analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers wipe out private student loan debt in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 42 House Democrats, sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its subcommittee for the rest of the 114th Congress and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current bankruptcy law, almost no student loan debt can be erased unless the borrower proves an 'undue hardship' — a standard so strict that even judges call it unclear, and it applies equally to private loans from banks just like federal loans. This bill would change that: private student loans (loans from banks and other for-profit lenders) would become dischargeable in bankruptcy like credit card debt, while federal and nonprofit-funded loans would keep the hardship protection. The bill was introduced in March 2015, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never moved again before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who took out private student loans and later fell into genuine financial distress. They would regain access to bankruptcy — a legal fresh start available on credit cards, medical bills, and most other unsecured debts — instead of carrying private loan debt for life. Their families also benefit, since private loans are often co-signed by parents who remain liable even after death or permanent disability of the borrower.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Section 523(a)(8) of the bankruptcy code so that only loans made or guaranteed by a government, or funded by a government or a nonprofit, are protected from discharge; purely private loans could be erased in bankruptcy like other consumer debts.

Borrowers would no longer have to prove 'undue hardship' to escape private student loan debt — a test so difficult that most distressed borrowers never even try, leaving them with debts they cannot pay and cannot escape.
The change would apply only to bankruptcy cases filed after enactment, so it would not disturb any existing arrangements.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders and investors, who would lose the guarantee that their loans are nearly impossible to escape in bankruptcy. Some loans would cost them more to make or would not be made at all to the riskiest borrowers, and some distressed borrowers' debts would be written down or wiped out.

drawbacks.text: Lenders would face higher losses in bankruptcy, and would likely respond by charging higher interest rates, requiring co-signers, or lending less to borrowers they consider risky — costs that would fall partly on future students.

Because private loans would become easier to discharge than federal loans under the amended law, the bill creates an asymmetry: it treats bank-issued loans more favorably in bankruptcy than government-backed ones, which some would argue inverts the usual rule that borrowers get more protection on public debt.
The bill does nothing to lower the cost of college or reduce borrowing before the fact; it addresses only what happens after a borrower is already in financial ruin.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers already in hardship, the benefit is real and large: a path out of debts that current law makes effectively permanent. The main cost is that private lenders may charge somewhat more or lend more cautiously, which affects future students at the margin. Weighing permanent, unpayable debt against slightly tighter credit terms for a slice of borrowers, the tradeoff favors the bill — though its narrower coverage of federal loans is a legitimate design criticism.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Judiciary Committee, was passed down to a subcommittee in April 2015, and then sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the remaining two years of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on March 26, 2015, with Reps. Danny Davis and Eric Swalwell as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On April 29, 2015, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action ever taken on it.

The bill accumulated 41 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or voted on it, and the full House never considered it before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders and loan investors are better off, because the bankruptcy protection that makes their loans nearly impossible to escape remained intact. Borrowers in distress are no better off than before.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 41 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 41 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction; chaired by Rep. Bob Goodlatte (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, and no report out of committee during the entire 114th Congress, leaving it at the subcommittee referral stage.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; because the bill never reached a vote, there is no roll-call record of where the full parties stood.

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders and investors
industries.note: The bill strips private lenders of the special bankruptcy shield that makes their loans more collectible than nearly any other consumer debt. Their interest in keeping that shield runs directly against distressed borrowers who want the same bankruptcy fresh start available on credit cards and medical bills.

industries.industry: Student loan debt collectors and buyers of charged-off loans
industries.note: Debts that could be discharged in bankruptcy would no longer be pursued, bought, and collected indefinitely, shrinking the market for aged private student loan paper.
